chapter: Los Angeles with Mutt Carey and the taxi dances
title: Copying Trumbauer's solo with Alex Hill's help
summary: Mutt cared about nobody but himself, but Alex Hill wrote out Trumbauer's solo for Joe, one of the few times he copied a solo.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Did you ever talk to Mutt about Bix Beiderbecke or that record of...
What did Mutt think about Bix Beiderbecke? Did he ever...

Mutt didn't think about nobody but himself! [LAUGHS] But believe me, everybody else did. In fact, you listen to that record, and they've got a hellified solo, Frankie Trumbauer, on "Singin' The Blues." [SINGS REFRAIN FROM SOLO] And Alex Hill... I couldn't quite pick it up by ear, you know. Alex Hill says, "Wait a minute. I'll

write it for you." He was a terrific arranger. So Alex Hill wrote me the whole thing, and I practiced it, and then I played it practically note for note like Trumbauer did. That was one of the few times I really wanted to copy a solo and play it.

I'm glad you said that. Because I think on the second tape we were saying that most of the New Orleans musicians didn't copy anybody; they had their own styles. But you right now say that you played that sort of note for note.

Well, yeah. It wasn't Trumbauer's style I wanted to copy so much, although I liked... I really liked his playing, but I never tried to copy his playing. This one particular solo, I wanted to play it. And I eventually probably could have picked it up just by listening. But Alex Hill said, "Well, I'll just write it out for you."
